result:
I think about the small things more than the big, because the small things are what keep circling back into everyday life. Tiny habits, moments of silence, the smell of rain on pavement—these are the things that accumulate into a sense of being alive. You can plan and map out a future, but what actually shapes your days is the ordinary, the mundane—how you tie your shoes, the way you drink your coffee, the timing of a laugh.

Sometimes it’s the end of a hallway that feels most like a beginning, not the starting line in a clean, white room. There’s something magnetic about the edge of a room, the place where light fades and shadows gather; it’s a reminder that you’re always in transition, always just beyond “arrived.” Those moments, the ones when you’re between two states, feel simultaneously fragile and infinite. Maybe that’s why we pause at thresholds. We’re listening.

Enough about edges—let’s talk about nonsense. What if the stars are just holes poked in the ceiling of some cosmic attic? Every so often, some dreamer takes a ladder, climbs up, and sticks their face through to remind themselves that there’s another room above. It doesn’t make practical sense, but then again, neither does crochet when you first see someone holding a needle and a looping yarn. There’s faith in making a pattern from nothing, the same faith you need to keep writing when the words refuse to fall into place.

The world isn’t falling apart. It’s being remade over and over somewhere in the texture of conversations, in the glimmer of a moment that doesn’t get recorded. You show up, you offer a joke, a hand, a dish of food, unknowingly altering someone else’s course. Maybe that’s all this is—chapter after chapter of gentle interruptions, of being unexpectedly seen.

It’s a beautiful mess, and we’re all just trying to remember the lyrics.
